title: Graphs
summary: Nodes and edges; adjacency list for sparse, matrix for dense.

parts.rule: A graph is a set of nodes plus a set of edges, directed or undirected, weighted or not. Represent sparse graphs with adjacency lists using space O(n + m). Represent dense graphs with an n by n matrix using space O(n²). Reachability walks come later; first pick a representation that matches density and direction.
parts.why: Both algorithm and system prompts start with "how do you store this." A matrix on a sparse social graph wastes memory; a list makes "is there an edge" a scan. Forgetting directed versus undirected silently breaks follow-graphs and dependency edges. Stating representation before the walk shows control.
parts.example: Undirected edges (1,2), (1,3), (2,4). Adjacency list: 1 maps to [2, 3], 2 maps to [1, 4], 3 maps to [1], 4 maps to [2]. Space tracks four nodes and six directed stubs for three undirected edges. A 4 by 4 matrix would store mostly zeros. "Neighbors of 1" scans a list of length two. "Does edge 2–3 exist?" with lists may scan neighbors of 2; with a matrix you read one cell in constant time. For a directed follow relation where 1 follows 2 but not reverse, store 1:[2] and 2:[] — direction is data, not decoration.
parts.use: Use adjacency lists for sparse social, map, and dependency graphs. Use a matrix when n is small and you need constant-time edge checks or dense all-pairs work. Use an explicit edge list when you will sort edges, as in Kruskal.
parts.refuse: Refuse a matrix for millions of sparse nodes. Refuse assuming undirected when the prompt is a follow or depends-on relation. Refuse storing only edges and dropping orphan nodes if isolated nodes matter. Refuse mutating a neighbor list while iterating it without a clear copy or index policy.

body:
Rule. A graph is a set of nodes plus a set of edges, directed or undirected, weighted or not. Represent sparse graphs with adjacency lists using space O(n + m). Represent dense graphs with an n by n matrix using space O(n²). Reachability walks come later; first pick a representation that matches density and direction.

Why it matters. Both algorithm and system prompts start with "how do you store this." A matrix on a sparse social graph wastes memory; a list makes "is there an edge" a scan. Forgetting directed versus undirected silently breaks follow-graphs and dependency edges. Stating representation before the walk shows control.

Worked example. Undirected edges (1,2), (1,3), (2,4). Adjacency list: 1 maps to [2, 3], 2 maps to [1, 4], 3 maps to [1], 4 maps to [2]. Space tracks four nodes and six directed stubs for three undirected edges. A 4 by 4 matrix would store mostly zeros. "Neighbors of 1" scans a list of length two. "Does edge 2–3 exist?" with lists may scan neighbors of 2; with a matrix you read one cell in constant time. For a directed follow relation where 1 follows 2 but not reverse, store 1:[2] and 2:[] — direction is data, not decoration.

When to use. Use adjacency lists for sparse social, map, and dependency graphs. Use a matrix when n is small and you need constant-time edge checks or dense all-pairs work. Use an explicit edge list when you will sort edges, as in Kruskal.

When to refuse. Refuse a matrix for millions of sparse nodes. Refuse assuming undirected when the prompt is a follow or depends-on relation. Refuse storing only edges and dropping orphan nodes if isolated nodes matter. Refuse mutating a neighbor list while iterating it without a clear copy or index policy.
